utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to put on the record that Mr. Mladic is not in court. He explicitly waived his right which was confirmed by counsel yesterday to be present when we would deal with administrative matters primarily today. I have two matters on my agenda. First, is to deliver a relatively short oral decision, and then to hear further submissions in relation to the authenticity of intercepts in relation to Witness RM507. Is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and counsel. There is one brief matter. This -- this regards an e-mail that the Prosecution sent yesterday afternoon that the Prosecution would just seek to put on the record; namely in compliance with the Trial Chamber's oral decision regarding the Prosecution's resubmission of the transcript evidence of Tarik Zunic, RM179, pursuant to Rule 92 bis. The Prosecution has uploaded into e-court this material now under 65 ter number 30511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It being uploaded, I think no number had yet been assigned to the previous version, the longer version, of the evidence of Mr. Zunic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30511 receives number P2980, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2980 is admitted into evidence under Rule 92 bis. Then I'll move to my first item, which is a decision of the Chamber on the tendering of a proposed exhibit with Rule 65 ter number 25116A. On the 2nd of May of this year, the Prosecution tendered Rule 65 ter 25116A in court with Witness Nicolai. This can be found at transcript page 10589. The Chamber will herein after refer to it as the proposed exhibit. On the same day, the Chamber delivered its decision on Prosecution's bar table motion for the admission of intercepts: Srebrenica segment, in which the Chamber did not take judicial notice of the authenticity of the proposed exhibit, and did not admit it at that time. The Chamber's view, given the tendering of the proposed exhibit in court with Witness Nicolai, is that the issue of its admission is still pending before the Chamber. At the outset, the Chamber emphasises that the clear distinction that exists between taking judicial notice of the authenticity of, for example, an intercept, and the requirements for admission when this same intercept is tendered in court with a witness who states that he or she was a participant in the intercepted conversation. The former requires that the Prosecution demonstrates that the authenticity of the document has been established in a previous trial. The latter requires, pursuant to Rule 89(C) of the Rules, that the document is relevant to the charges in the indictment and of probative value. The Prosecution submits that the proposed exhibit is an audio version of an intercepted conversation which has already been admitted into evidence as P1186. Upon review, the Chamber is satisfied that, while the transcription of the audio and the text of P1186 differ in terms of length and detail, they both relate to the same conversation. The proposed exhibit appears to be a conversation regarding the evacuation of a UN DutchBat soldier who had been shot and killed. Witness Nicolai testified that he was a participant in this conversation when shown P1186 in court. Given that the proposed exhibit appears to be a more comprehensive version of P1186, the Chamber is satisfied that it is sufficiently relevant and of probative value for admission into evidence. The Chamber therefore admits into evidence Rule 65 ter number 25116A and requests the Registry to assign this document an exhibit number. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to this objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. These intercepts are relevant to members -- first of all, to the members of the alleged JCE and they also relate to contextualising events that do arise within the indictment period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, apart from the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Covers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next objection is, at that time, all these intercepts cover territory on which General Mladic was not present. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just very briefly Mr. President. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any further objections or comments on the tendered 153 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1991. Thank you, Your Honour. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That Mr. Karadzic was able to influence something. Has nothing to do with General Mladic, especially not in 1991. There is no mention of General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it says that it is also relevant to Karadzic's preparation for the establishment of an ethnically Serb MUP and to his long-standing relationship with Tomo Kovac. That's how I understand, at least, the relevance as you explain it -- as the Prosecution explains it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's correct. This -- this relates to JCE members and allegations regarding the JCE. And I may just remind my learned colleague that at this stage we are dealing with the admissibility of evidence. We are not dealing with any final findings of fact. We are not really at the point of that by quite a wide margin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But in order to have probative value it should be relevant and relevance certainly is a matter which plays a role at the admission stage, unless you would disagree with that, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I would absolutely agree, Mr. President. And for that reason, we have articulated the relevance and the articulation is relevant to our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is a different argument than the one you used a second ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I summarised, which I'll not do any further, what I understand to be the explained relevance. We leave it to Mr. Shin to explain that in further detail. But I asked you to choose the three strongest examples of where you challenged the relevance as explained by the Prosecution. You've chosen the first one. Could you, in view of these submissions made by Mr. Shin, tell us why he is wrong in considering this to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Everything is interconnected, of course, especially in a small country as Bosnia. Then, if we go by that logic, everything is relevant. We are telling and claiming that Mr. Mladic had no dealings whatsoever before May, probably 9th, and for sure 12th, with anybody in Bosnia-Herzegovina. His chain of command was coming from federal state, from Belgrade, and he was in Croatia. He had nothing to do with any authority in Bosnia, nothing whatsoever, before he came to Bosnia. He could not know what's going on there, since he was emerged in -- he was in the middle of the war in Croatia. He had much better -- much more serious concerns with his direct surrounding, with his troops under attack, inside barracks all over Croatia; actually in Croatian Krajisnik. So I'm sure that he did not follow the news from Bosnia because he had no time nor was he interested in what's going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time. And claiming that he has anything to do with this while he was in the middle of the war in another part of then-federal state is -- is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Positions of the parties seem to be clear. I invited you to take the two or three of your strongest examples, or would you want to leave it to this more general observation?

utterances.text: I'll -- for example, general because we really can go one by one --

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry, I hadn't realised that the -- yeah. Basically the Prosecution reiterates its position as to the relevance, which is set out here, and Mr. Lukic has not addressed the arguments.

utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Well, then, let's give an opportunity for Mr. Lukic to deal with number 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment you're commenting on content rather on relevance. Any --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It cannot show the position of General Mladic in 1991, at all. Neither what he thought nor what he did. And, again, we reiterate it has nothing do with him. Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's it, then we'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Moloto has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is it the position of the Defence that in a case like this one, where JCE is also alleged, that the Prosecution is precluded from showing the conduct of the so-called JCE members, even if, at the time -- the time-frame has nothing to do with the indictment but it shows the context within which the indictment acts were committed?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, that we don't -- do not claim that they cannot show context and that they cannot show what alleged co-perpetrators in JCE are doing, but they have to show what role General Mladic has in -- in this context as well. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

So -- then if we want to show his dealings or his relationship with the situation that was created before that, there has to be some relationship shown, some context, in which you can find him. However, the -- as explained, and I can get the specific references - maybe not at my fingertips right now - we had sought to -- to be -- to indicate that the value of doing this would be that if the parties, including the Chamber at some point down the -- further in the proceedings, wish to tender further intercepts from this collection the witness would not need to be recalled. There would not need be to further authentication, that we would already have the foundation authentication for the intercepts there. In this regard, we had specifically noted that the Defence had used one intercept from this collection with a witness, and that was in open session, Witness John Wilson, and we had invited the -- the Defence to indicate any other intercepts that they had wished to authentic or, in fact, tender at this stage. But that was the rationale behind that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the -- of course, the question arises whether that rationale still applies. We are close to the end of the Prosecution's case, so, therefore, whatever intercepts the Prosecution would like to -- to present is -- should be known by now, more or less. And then, if the Defence, during the Defence case, or the Prosecution, during the Defence case, if there will be a Defence case, wants to rely on any of the others, we could, so to say, re-open that box if we would close all the irrelevant boxes at this very moment which means striking any comments which are not relative to authenticity or redacting anything which is not related to any tendered document. That document still is there in its unredacted format and could be used in the future, if need be, but then just for that relevant portion. The problem is that if the Chamber has 600 comments on intercepts before it, the Chamber is always inclined to carefully verify what that evidence is about, whether it's accurate, what it brings us, and for 75 per cent, it would be totally wasted time to work on that. That's the reason why the Chamber, at this moment, is considering to invite the Prosecution to redact everything which has not yet become relevant. Not to say that the chart still exists and can be re-called, if we could say so, at any later stage, if need be, for any intercept which would come up in the future. And -- but before the Chamber does so I'd like to hear your observations on what I just brought to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: May I just have one moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if you have developed any thoughts on that, of course, you are free to express them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President. You have, indeed, articulated the -- the -- the Prosecution did have in mind not only the Prosecution case, of course, but the Defence case and -- if any, and any other stage of the proceedings. One thing that we would propose is that this process of -- if I may make two points. One is that the chart of the 153 intercepts do not duplicate, to avoid duplication, do not list intercepts that are currently otherwise pending before other bar table motions or through other pending 92 bis or 92 quater witnesses. So to that extent there would be some authentication irrelevant there. But with that, we would propose that it may also be possible to present this process of redaction at the end of the case, if that would be acceptable to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the end of the Prosecution's case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: At the end of the case when the parties have -- at the end of the case as a whole, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then at least it would be necessary to know at this stage what has gained relevance already and what is there, still, if I could say so, on reserve not to be relied on, to be skipped, if not at a later stage it would have revived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, if I may briefly, Mr. President. We had sought to address this issue of specificity regarding individual intercepts by providing in the -- in original filing but also in the CD-ROM a correlation chart, of course, to show exactly which RM65 ter number would relate to which intercept on that large chart. We had sought to address this through that so that the attention of the parties and of the Chamber may be drawn to the specific -- specific intercept on that chart and that -- perhaps that addresses the concern that Your Honours have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it partly does; partly it does not. It is, if you say, We've drawn your attention to certain specific intercepts, then that doesn't mean that the others are not any further in evidence. I mean, you seem to ignore, more or less, that what is in evidence, the Chamber should consider that. And, therefore, we are seeking to end up in a situation where only material which turned out to have been relevant is in evidence is before this Chamber. Now, I can imagine that the parties would sit together, and with the guidance of the Chamber at this moment, find a technical solution so as that everything which has not been shown to be relevant up till this moment is off the table. At the same time, that the information of all that material which is now in reserve lying on the ground next to the table that that still can be reactivated, if need be, and to find a technical solution for that. Not to say, We've drawn your attention to this and this and this and therefore focus on that. The Chamber wants to be fed with material and should receive in evidence material that has been shown to be relevant. May I invite the parties to -- of course, the most important would be to look at 2566 again; 2567 is different because that's all about intercepts that are tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. On that second point, that's correct Mr. President. And, yes, we will attempt again to -- to discuss these matters with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the issue is now slightly different for your discussions. That is, that the Chamber wants to get -- don't -- doesn't want to have in evidence any material just because, in future, it may gain some relevance. That's something the Chamber does not accept at this moment and then to find a technical solution as where to store the -- the columns and the rows in reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other matter to be raised? If not, we will adjourn for the day, and we will resume Monday, the -- and let's see what Monday is. I think it's the 1st of December. We start at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 2nd of December. Yes. I should have known that because Thursday, the 5th, is Sint Nicolaas. You should keep that in mind as well. 2nd of December we freshly start again being at P exhibits, 3000. And we will resume in Courtroom II at 9.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd of December, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.04 p.m.,
